messages.content: I want to investigate causal effect identifiability reasoning from diagrams, especially whether a system can distinguish a structural edit from an equivalent redrawing across unseen graph compositions.

The distinction is between a change to the causal structure and a change only to how that structure is pictured. An edited diagram may warrant a different identifiability judgment; an equivalent redrawing represents the same graph and should preserve that judgment. The goal is to make that distinction even for graph compositions not previously encountered.
What should the investigation be aiming for quantitatively?

It has two stated targets: achieve 85% paired accuracy on identifiability judgments before and after structural edits, including cases with latent confounding; and maintain 95% prediction consistency across equivalent redrawings of held-out graph compositions. Those are targets, not results already established.
Why emphasize the judgments before and after an edit as a pair?

Because the question concerns reasoning about what the edit does to identifiability. Looking at the before-and-after judgments together keeps attention on both diagrams and their relationship, rather than only on an isolated verdict for one diagram. The 85% target is specifically for that paired setting.
Does a structural edit necessarily flip the answer?

No. It changes something about the graph's structure, but the causal effect might remain identifiable, remain non-identifiable, or change status. The relevant question is whether the edit changes the conditions that support the particular identifiability judgment, not whether every edit produces a different label.
And an equivalent redrawing is different because nothing causal has changed?

Exactly. If the graph is merely redrawn while preserving its nodes, directed relationships, and any represented latent-confounding relationships, the identifiability question is unchanged. The layout might look different, but the prediction should be consistent. That is what the 95% consistency target tests across equivalent redrawings of held-out graph compositions.
Could the two targets tell us different things?

Yes. Paired accuracy asks whether the before-and-after identifiability judgments are correct when structure is edited. Redrawing consistency asks whether predictions remain stable when structure is *not* edited. A system could be stable across redrawings yet consistently make an incorrect identifiability judgment; conversely, it could sometimes reach a correct judgment while being distracted by a different visual layout. Neither target substitutes for the other.
I also want latent confounding to remain explicit in the first target.

It is explicitly included: the 85% paired-accuracy target covers structural-edit cases including latent confounding. A latent common cause can matter to whether a causal effect is identifiable, so the reasoning cannot treat every apparent relationship in a diagram as though all relevant causes were observed. Its presence does not, by itself, settle every identifiability question.
Can you give a general illustration without assuming a particular graph in the investigation?

Suppose a diagram asks about the effect of X on Y. In general, changing a relationship in that diagram, or changing whether a common cause of X and Y is represented as latent, could change the reasoning needed to identify the effect. Merely moving X and Y to different places on the page while preserving the same relationships would not. That illustrates the conceptual distinction; it does not specify any of the graph compositions to be investigated or imply a verdict for them.
So the target is reasoning about identifiability, not estimating the size of an effect?

Right. An identifiability judgment asks whether the causal effect can be determined under the diagram's causal assumptions and the relevant observational information. It is distinct from calculating a numerical effect estimate or deciding that the effect is large, small, or zero. The stated accuracy and consistency targets concern identifiability predictions.
How should I understand “unseen graph compositions” here?

The goal is not limited to recognizing diagrams whose overall composition is already familiar. It calls for distinguishing edits from equivalent redrawings across unseen graph compositions. The 95% consistency requirement specifically refers to equivalent redrawings of held-out graph compositions. The statement does not specify which compositions they are or how they are assembled.
Would matching predictions on two redrawings prove that the predictions are right?

No. Matching predictions establish consistency between those equivalent views, not correctness of the identifiability judgment. That is why it matters to keep the 95% redrawing-consistency target separate from the 85% paired-accuracy target for before-and-after structural edits.
What if a structural edit happens to leave the answer unchanged? I don't want that mistaken for an equivalent redrawing.

An unchanged identifiability verdict does not mean the graphs are equivalent. Structural equivalence concerns what causal relationships the diagrams represent; identifiability is a judgment about the effect under those relationships. Two structurally different diagrams can receive the same verdict, whereas equivalent redrawings represent the same structure even if they look different.
And a visually dramatic redraw could still be equivalent?

Yes. Visual difference alone is not evidence of a structural edit. If the causal structure is preserved, a dramatic change in placement or presentation remains an equivalent redrawing for this purpose. Predictions should be consistent across such redrawings of held-out graph compositions, with 95% as the stated target.
Can you put the full aim together once more without implying it has already been achieved?

The aim is to investigate whether causal effect identifiability reasoning from diagrams tracks causal structure rather than superficial appearance across unseen graph compositions. Its targets are 85% paired accuracy on identifiability judgments before and after structural edits, including latent confounding, and 95% prediction consistency across equivalent redrawings of held-out graph compositions. Both remain goals, not reported outcomes.

For the diagram-based identifiability question, I propose training a diagram-to-ADMG encoder using ID-algorithm labels, structural-edit contrastive pairs, and redraw-invariance regularization on held-out graph compositions.

That proposal brings the three distinctions into one approach. The encoder would connect a visual diagram to an acyclic directed mixed graph, or ADMG; ID-algorithm labels would provide a basis for identifiability judgments; structural-edit contrastive pairs would emphasize changes to causal structure; and redraw-invariance regularization would encourage stability when the same structure is drawn differently. It is a proposed training approach, not an observed result.
Why use an ADMG as the intermediate representation?

An ADMG provides a graph representation in which directed relationships and relationships representing latent confounding can be distinguished. That makes it a relevant target for an encoder whose input is a diagram and whose downstream question is causal effect identifiability. The proposal does not specify an encoder architecture or a particular diagram format.
Does diagram-to-ADMG mean the model should just copy where things appear on the page?

No. The intended distinction is between visual placement and the relationships represented by the diagram. An equivalent redrawing can move things around without changing the ADMG it expresses. A structural edit, by contrast, can change the represented relationships even if the overall picture looks similar.
Where do the ID-algorithm labels fit?

They supply labels for the identifiability aspect of training. The ID algorithm concerns whether a causal effect is identifiable from a causal graph under the relevant assumptions. Using its labels ties the proposal to identifiability reasoning rather than merely to recognizing diagram features. No particular set of graphs, effects, or label-generation procedure is specified here.
So an ID-algorithm label isn't a numerical estimate of the effect?

Correct. In this proposal, the labels concern identifiability: whether the effect can be identified under the represented causal structure. They should not be read as measured effect sizes or as claims about the magnitude of an effect.
What role do the structural-edit contrastive pairs play alongside those labels?

They make the comparison between a diagram before an edit and a diagram after that edit explicit. The training proposal can then emphasize attention to what changed structurally, while the ID-algorithm labels address the associated identifiability judgments. The proposal does not say that every structural edit must change the identifiability label.
If both members of a structural-edit pair receive the same identifiability label, is the pair still meaningful?

Yes. The diagrams can be structurally different while the answer to the particular identifiability question remains the same. A contrastive pair identifies an edit to the represented graph; it does not assert that the edit necessarily flips the judgment. Preserving that distinction is important for reasoning about the edit rather than assuming a label change.
And redraw-invariance regularization is for the opposite sort of comparison?

It addresses equivalent redrawings: visually different depictions that preserve the represented causal structure. The proposed regularization encourages predictions to remain stable across those depictions, rather than treating a change in layout as a change in the graph. The node places this regularization on held-out graph compositions, without specifying the precise regularizer or how those compositions are organized.
I want to be careful with the phrase “held-out graph compositions.” Does the proposal say exactly how those are selected?

No. It specifies redraw-invariance regularization on held-out graph compositions but gives no selection rule, split definition, or training schedule. Those details should not be inferred from the phrase alone. What is explicit is the intended invariance across equivalent redrawings in that held-out-composition setting.
How do latent confounding and the ADMG choice connect?

An ADMG can represent directed causal relationships while also expressing confounding relationships associated with latent variables, commonly through bidirected edges. That allows the proposal to address diagrams where latent confounding matters to identifiability. It does not assert that any particular diagram with latent confounding has an identifiable or non-identifiable effect.
Would redraw invariance still apply if a redrawing makes a confounding relationship look less visually prominent?

If it is genuinely an equivalent redrawing, it preserves that relationship regardless of how prominent it looks. The regularization is aimed at stability under changes of presentation, not at ignoring represented confounding. Removing or altering the relationship would be a structural change instead.
Could an edit be visually subtle but structurally important?

Yes. The visual size of a change does not determine its causal significance. A subtle alteration to a represented relationship can be a structural edit, whereas a conspicuous rearrangement can leave the graph unchanged. The proposed contrastive pairs and redraw-invariance regularization target those different possibilities.
How does this proposal relate to the accuracy and consistency targets we discussed?

It is a proposed way to pursue them, not evidence that either has been met. ID-algorithm labels and structural-edit contrastive pairs relate to the target of 85% paired accuracy on identifiability judgments before and after structural edits, including latent confounding. Redraw-invariance regularization relates to the target of 95% prediction consistency across equivalent redrawings of held-out graph compositions.
Does using the ID algorithm by itself guarantee consistent predictions from redrawn diagrams?

No. The ID algorithm operates on a graph representation, while the proposal begins with diagrams that must be interpreted. If equivalent drawings are encoded differently in ways that affect the judgment, algorithm-derived labels alone do not resolve the visual-invariance issue. That is the separate role proposed for redraw-invariance regularization.
Likewise, could redraw consistency alone establish that the encoder got the causal structure right?

No. Consistently treating two drawings the same does not establish that either was interpreted correctly. The proposal combines graph-oriented encoding, ID-algorithm labels, edit comparisons, and redraw invariance because these address related but distinct aspects of the reasoning problem.
Should I describe this as a finished method with a specified loss function?

Not from the stated proposal. It specifies the training ingredients and the diagram-to-ADMG aim, but not a loss formula, model architecture, graph collection, or measured performance. It is accurate to call it a proposed training approach; adding those particulars would go beyond what has been specified.
Then the central idea is to learn from actual structural differences without treating equivalent drawings as different causal cases?

Yes. More precisely, the proposal is to train a diagram-to-ADMG encoder with ID-algorithm labels and structural-edit contrastive pairs, while using redraw-invariance regularization on held-out graph compositions. That combination is meant to keep identifiability judgments sensitive to represented causal structure and insensitive to equivalent changes in presentation, without presuming the targets have already been achieved.
Can the diagram-to-ADMG encoder distinguish added latent confounding from visually rerouted, structurally unchanged edges in held-out graph compositions?

That is the question to resolve; the information so far does not establish whether it can. Added latent confounding changes the causal structure represented by a diagram. Visually rerouting an edge, while keeping its endpoints and meaning unchanged, changes only its appearance. The encoder would need to respond to the first difference without treating the second as a new graph.
What exactly counts as a visually rerouted edge in this question?

An edge whose drawn path changes but whose structural relationship does not. For example, a line might take a different route across the page yet still connect the same nodes in the same way. If its direction and any indication of confounding are also preserved, the change is visual rather than structural.
So the line's shape is not itself the causal relationship?

Right. The causal relationship is conveyed by what the edge represents, including its endpoints and type, not by whether the line is straight or curved. A rerouted line can look quite different while leaving the graph unchanged.
How is added latent confounding different from that?

It adds a represented confounding relationship rather than merely changing how an existing edge is drawn. In an ADMG, latent confounding can be expressed by a bidirected relationship between nodes. Adding such a relationship is a structural change, even if it is visually small or drawn near other edges.
Does adding latent confounding automatically change the identifiability judgment?

Not automatically. It changes the structure that identifiability reasoning must consider, but whether the judgment changes depends on the causal-effect question and the rest of the graph. The encoder question is first about distinguishing the structural addition from a nonstructural rerouting, not about assuming that every such addition flips an identifiability label.
If the identifiability label stays the same, could the encoder still have missed the added confounding?

Yes, the same final label would not by itself show whether the added relationship was represented correctly. Structurally different graphs can have the same identifiability judgment for a particular effect. Distinguishing the diagrams as graphs and producing an identifiability judgment are related, but they are not identical questions.
And if two rerouted drawings receive the same judgment, does that prove the encoder understood them as the same graph?

No. Equal judgments alone establish only agreement on that output. The encoder could, in principle, arrive at the same judgment from different representations. The question here is more specific: can it keep structurally unchanged edges unchanged in its ADMG interpretation while recognizing added latent confounding as a structural difference?
Why specify held-out graph compositions?

It asks whether the distinction carries over to compositions outside the ones at issue in training, rather than depending on familiarity with a particular overall arrangement. The node does not state which compositions are held out or report how the encoder performs on them.
Could a rerouted edge be mistaken for an added confounding relationship just because it crosses another line?

That illustrates the visual ambiguity the question is concerned with. A crossing or a changed route is not, on its own, an added causal relationship. What matters is whether the diagram actually represents a new relationship, rather than simply drawing an existing edge along a different path. This is a conceptual distinction, not a report that the encoder makes that particular mistake.
What if the rerouted line comes close to a different node?

Proximity alone should not determine the graph. If the edge still has the same endpoints and type, coming close to another node does not make it connect to that node. But whether a particular encoder maintains that distinction in held-out graph compositions remains an open question here.
Does the question require the encoder to ignore everything visual?

No. It has to read a visual diagram to determine what relationships are represented. The issue is using visual information appropriately: attend to features that specify connections and relationship types, without treating a different route for an unchanged edge as a different causal structure.
Could you state the two cases side by side without implying a test result?

In the added-latent-confounding case, the diagram represents a relationship that was not present before, so its ADMG representation changes. In the visually rerouted-edge case, the same relationship is drawn differently, so its ADMG representation remains structurally unchanged. The open question is whether the diagram-to-ADMG encoder preserves that distinction on held-out graph compositions.
Is it enough for it to notice that one picture has more ink or a different-looking line?

No. Those visual differences need not track causal differences. The meaningful distinction is whether a latent-confounding relationship has been added or an existing edge has merely been rerouted. An answer based only on how different the pictures look would not address the question.
How does this connect to the identifiability reasoning we discussed earlier?

The ADMG interpretation is relevant because identifiability reasoning depends on the represented causal structure. Added latent confounding may alter the reasoning needed for a causal-effect judgment; rerouting an unchanged edge should not alter that reasoning. The present question asks whether the encoder can tell those inputs apart at the structural level before drawing conclusions about its identifiability predictions.
So I shouldn't answer ‘yes’ merely because the training proposal included redraw invariance and structural-edit pairs?

Correct. Those are proposed ingredients intended to address the distinction. They do not establish the encoder's behavior on held-out graph compositions. Whether it actually distinguishes added latent confounding from visually rerouted, structurally unchanged edges remains unanswered in the information provided.
And I shouldn't answer ‘no’ just because the two kinds of diagram change might look similar?

Correct. Visual similarity can make the distinction important, but it does not establish failure either. The question concerns whether the encoder tracks the relationship represented by each diagram, rather than visual change alone; no outcome has been stated.
My hypothesis is that contrastive ADMG training will achieve ≥85% paired accuracy for latent-confounder edits and ≥95% redraw consistency on unseen compositions.

That is a prediction, not a reported result. It addresses the question of whether the encoder can respond to added latent confounding while remaining stable when an edge is only drawn differently. The two thresholds cover different behaviors: accurate before-and-after judgments for latent-confounder edits, and consistent predictions across equivalent redrawings on unseen compositions.
Should I keep the greater-than-or-equal-to signs?
Yes. The hypothesis says at least 85% paired accuracy and at least 95% redraw consistency. It does not predict exactly 85% or exactly 95%.
What does “paired accuracy” refer to here?

It refers to identifiability judgments considered together for a diagram before and after a latent-confounder edit. The hypothesis sets a ≥85% target for those pairs. It does not say that the edit must change the identifiability answer in every pair.
So a pair might be judged correctly even if both diagrams have the same identifiability status?

Yes. Adding latent confounding changes the represented graph, but the effect under consideration need not switch from identifiable to non-identifiable, or vice versa, in every case. The paired judgment needs to reflect the correct status of each diagram, whether the statuses differ or coincide.
How does the redraw-consistency part differ?

That part concerns diagrams that represent the same structure despite a change in appearance. The hypothesis predicts ≥95% consistency of predictions across equivalent redrawings on unseen compositions. Unlike a latent-confounder edit, an equivalent redrawing does not add a causal relationship.
Does the hypothesis say the encoder will recognize every added confounder?

No. A threshold of ≥85% paired accuracy does not assert flawless performance on every latent-confounder edit. Nor does it, by itself, establish that every intermediate ADMG representation is correct. It states a predicted level of performance for paired identifiability judgments.
And ≥95% consistency still permits some inconsistent predictions?

Yes. It predicts a high level of consistency, not perfect invariance. It also concerns agreement across equivalent redrawings; agreement alone does not establish that the shared identifiability judgment is correct.
I want the hypothesis to speak to the question about visually rerouted edges without changing its wording too much.

Redraw consistency is the part that bears on visually rerouted, structurally unchanged edges: changing an edge's drawn route should not change a prediction when its represented relationship is preserved. Paired accuracy for latent-confounder edits bears on the structurally changed case. Together, the predicted thresholds address both sides of the question, though neither is an observed answer to it.
Could the two predicted thresholds come apart?

Conceptually, yes. An encoder might be consistent across redrawings yet inaccurate about the identifiability judgments around latent-confounder edits. Or it might handle many edit pairs correctly while changing its prediction when an equivalent diagram is redrawn. The hypothesis predicts that contrastive ADMG training reaches both stated thresholds.
Does “on unseen compositions” qualify only the second number?

As stated, the hypothesis explicitly attaches “on unseen compositions” to ≥95% redraw consistency. It specifies ≥85% paired accuracy for latent-confounder edits, without separately spelling out a composition condition for that measure. I would preserve that wording rather than silently add a qualification.
Is this a hypothesis about the causal effects themselves?

No. It predicts performance on reasoning about whether causal effects are identifiable from diagrams. The percentages concern paired accuracy and prediction consistency; they are not estimates of an effect's size or of how often latent confounding occurs.
What exactly is the structural contrast behind the first prediction?

A latent-confounder edit adds a represented confounding relationship, so the before and after diagrams differ in causal structure. Contrastive ADMG training is hypothesized to help with the paired identifiability judgments across that change. The hypothesis does not specify particular graphs, edits, or outcomes for individual pairs.
Could a visually rerouted edge look more different than an added confounding relationship?

It could, in general. That is why the distinction cannot rest on the amount of visual change. The hypothesis is about responding appropriately to the represented structure: a latent-confounder edit may matter to identifiability reasoning, while an equivalent rerouting should leave the prediction consistent.
If both thresholds were reached, would that settle whether every encoded ADMG is faithful to its diagram?

No. Those aggregate performance thresholds would bear on the stated identifiability and consistency behaviors, but they would not, on their own, prove that every diagram was encoded perfectly. The hypothesis makes no claim of perfect graph reconstruction.
If neither threshold has been measured here, how should I phrase the claim?

Keep it conditional in status but definite as a prediction: “We hypothesize that contrastive ADMG training will achieve ≥85% paired accuracy for latent-confounder edits and ≥95% redraw consistency on unseen compositions.” That preserves both numerical thresholds and avoids presenting them as findings.
Is the hypothesis saying latent confounding can be ignored whenever the final judgment happens to stay the same?

No. The addition remains a structural edit even if the correct identifiability status happens not to change for a particular effect. The paired-accuracy prediction concerns getting the judgments right on both sides of such edits; it does not redefine an unchanged judgment as evidence that the edit was merely visual.
Then what would be an overstatement when describing the redraw part?

Saying that the encoder is completely invariant to all visual changes would overstate it. The hypothesis is specifically ≥95% prediction consistency across equivalent redrawings on unseen compositions. It does not cover arbitrary alterations that change the graph, and it does not claim 100% consistency.
Does this hypothesis already answer the earlier question with a yes?

Not yet. It predicts performance relevant to that question: ≥85% paired accuracy for latent-confounder edits and ≥95% consistency when equivalent diagrams are redrawn on unseen compositions. Until those predictions are assessed, it remains a hypothesis about the encoder's ability to distinguish structural confounding changes from purely visual rerouting.
I plan to generate held-out ADMG compositions with confounder edits and equivalent redraws, train the diagram-to-ADMG encoder, and then measure paired accuracy and redraw consistency.

That sequence directly addresses the question about distinguishing added confounding from changes that only affect how an edge is drawn. The confounder edits provide structural changes to reason about; the equivalent redraws provide visually different presentations of unchanged structure. After training the encoder, paired accuracy and redraw consistency would measure those two aspects separately. This is a plan, not a completed evaluation.
What does generating the held-out compositions contribute?

It puts the distinction in graph compositions that are held out, rather than asking only about a familiar overall diagram. The plan does not specify which compositions to generate or how to select them. What matters here is that they support both comparisons: a confounder edit and an equivalent redrawing.
Are a confounder edit and an equivalent redraw two ways of changing the same thing?

No. A confounder edit changes a relationship represented in the ADMG. An equivalent redraw changes the picture while preserving the represented graph. The plan includes both because the encoder should be assessed for sensitivity to a structural difference and stability under a nonstructural visual difference.
Does the plan require the confounder edit to change the identifiability answer?

No. It requires confounder edits as structural comparisons, but a structural change does not necessarily change the identifiability judgment for a particular causal effect. Measuring paired accuracy means considering whether the before-and-after judgments are correct, not assuming they must differ.
And an equivalent redraw should leave the identifiability question itself unchanged?

Yes. If it is equivalent, the causal relationships represented by the diagram remain the same. The drawing can change, but the identifiability question under that graph does not. Redraw consistency measures whether the encoder's predictions remain stable across those presentations.
What is the significance of measuring the two outcomes after training?

Training is the proposed preparation of the encoder; measurement is how its behavior on the planned comparisons would be assessed. The order matters because a training proposal does not itself establish how the trained encoder will perform. The plan says to measure paired accuracy and redraw consistency afterward, without reporting either value.
Could I collapse both measurements into one general score for whether it handles diagram changes?

That would lose the distinction the plan is designed to examine. Paired accuracy concerns identifiability judgments before and after confounder edits. Redraw consistency concerns prediction agreement when the graph is unchanged despite a different drawing. Keeping them separate makes clear whether a measured behavior relates to structural edits or equivalent redraws.
If predictions match across redraws, can I infer that the encoder represented the ADMG correctly?

Not from matching predictions alone. Consistency says the outputs agree across equivalent drawings; the same judgment could still be incorrect. That is why the plan also measures accuracy on paired identifiability judgments. Neither measurement alone is a claim that every internal graph representation is correct.
If paired accuracy is measured, does that by itself show the encoder ignores irrelevant visual rerouting?

No. Correct judgments around confounder edits would address one side of the question, but would not establish stability across different drawings of an unchanged graph. Measuring redraw consistency separately addresses that side.
Should the equivalent redraws be treated as structural edits just because they look different?

No. Their defining feature in this plan is that they are equivalent: the represented ADMG stays structurally unchanged. Treating them as edits would erase the comparison between a genuine confounding change and a change of presentation.
Does generating ADMG compositions mean the encoder's inputs stop being diagrams?

No. The encoder is still diagram-to-ADMG. The generated ADMG compositions identify the graph structures at issue, while the equivalent redraws concern their diagrammatic presentation. The plan does not specify the mechanics for producing those drawings or the encoder's architecture.
How much can we say about how training and the held-out compositions interact?

Only what the plan states: generate held-out ADMG compositions with the two kinds of comparison, train the encoder, and then measure the two outcomes. “Held-out” indicates that the compositions serve to probe behavior beyond compositions used for training, but the plan gives no detailed partition, schedule, or training procedure.
Could a confounder edit be visually subtle while an equivalent redraw is visually dramatic?

Yes, in principle. That is why the two categories are defined by what happens to the represented graph, not by how noticeable a change looks. The planned measurements ask whether the encoder responds appropriately to that structural distinction.
Does this plan already tell us whether the encoder can make the distinction?

No. It lays out how to examine the question: use held-out ADMG compositions with confounder edits and equivalent redraws, train the encoder, and measure paired accuracy and redraw consistency. The encoder's actual performance is not stated.
Then when describing the plan, I should avoid language like “the encoder remains consistent across redraws”?

Yes. That would present a hoped-for behavior as an observed one. The accurate phrasing is that you plan to measure whether its predictions remain consistent across equivalent redraws, alongside paired accuracy for the confounder edits.
The activity is to train the diagram-to-ADMG encoder on 12,000 ID-labeled ADMG diagrams, then measure confounder-edit paired accuracy and redraw consistency across 2,000 held-out compositions.

That specifies both the training material and the scope of the measurements. The encoder is trained on 12,000 ID-labeled ADMG diagrams. Confounder-edit paired accuracy and redraw consistency are then measured across 2,000 held-out compositions. The numbers count different things: training diagrams in the first case and held-out compositions in the second.
What does “ID-labeled” tell us about the diagrams?

It says their labels come from the ID algorithm and concern causal effect identifiability under the represented graph. It does not mean that the labels are numerical estimates of causal effects, or specify which effects are queried for each diagram.
Why call it a diagram-to-ADMG encoder if the training items are already described as ADMG diagrams?

Because an ADMG diagram is a visual depiction of a graph, while the encoder's task is to interpret that depiction as graph structure. Describing the training items as ADMG diagrams identifies what they represent; it does not make visual interpretation unnecessary.
Should I say there are 12,000 training compositions?
No. The stated count is 12,000 ID-labeled ADMG diagrams used to train the encoder. It does not specify how many distinct graph compositions those diagrams represent.
Likewise, are the 2,000 held-out compositions necessarily 2,000 pictures?

That does not follow from the wording. The count is of held-out compositions, not of drawings. Measuring redraw consistency involves equivalent visual presentations, but the activity does not state a total number of pictures or redraws.
What is paired in the confounder-edit accuracy measurement?

The identifiability judgments on the before-and-after sides of a confounder edit. The measurement concerns whether those judgments are correct as a pair. An edit changes the represented confounding structure, but it need not change the identifiability answer in every pair.
Does the activity specify how many confounder-edit pairs there are?

No. It specifies that confounder-edit paired accuracy is measured across the 2,000 held-out compositions, but it does not give a separate pair count or say how many edits are associated with each composition.
What would redraw consistency measure in the same activity?

It measures whether predictions agree across equivalent drawings of a represented graph. The drawings may look different, but an equivalent redraw leaves the graph's structure unchanged. The activity names redraw consistency as a measurement; it does not report a consistency value.
Could the two measurements be treated as interchangeable?

No. Confounder-edit paired accuracy concerns correctness around a structural change. Redraw consistency concerns stability when presentation changes but structure does not. Reporting one would not, by itself, state the other.
Is latent confounding relevant in both cases?

It is explicit in the confounder-edit measurement: that measurement concerns edits to represented confounding. For an equivalent redraw, any represented confounding relationship must remain the same if the redraw is truly equivalent. The consistency question is whether a different presentation changes the prediction despite that unchanged structure.
What if an edge takes a different route in the redrawn picture?

If its endpoints and relationship type remain unchanged, a different route is a visual change, not a confounder edit. Redraw consistency is the relevant measurement for predictions across those equivalent presentations. The activity does not state what predictions the encoder makes in such cases.
And if a latent-confounding relationship is added, should that go in the redraw comparison?

No. Adding that relationship changes the represented ADMG. It belongs with structural confounder-edit comparisons, even if the visual change is small. An equivalent redraw preserves the relationship structure.
Do the ID labels alone tell us how the encoder will respond to a rerouted line?

No. ID labels concern identifiability under a represented graph. How the encoder interprets different drawings is a separate aspect of its behavior, which is why redraw consistency is measured rather than inferred from the presence of labels.
Does training on 12,000 diagrams mean the encoder has already reached any particular accuracy?
The activity specifies a training count, not a measured performance result. Its performance on confounder-edit pairs and equivalent redraws is what the subsequent measurements are meant to describe.
Can you phrase the sequence without making the measurements sound completed?

Train the diagram-to-ADMG encoder on 12,000 ID-labeled ADMG diagrams, then measure confounder-edit paired accuracy and redraw consistency across 2,000 held-out compositions. This states the activity and its order without supplying outcomes.
What details should remain open in that description?

It does not specify the encoder architecture, the number of redraws or edit pairs, how the compositions are selected, or the measured values. Keeping those details open preserves the stated activity without filling in procedures or results that have not been supplied.
On 2,000 held-out ADMG compositions, confounder-edit paired accuracy reached 87%, and equivalent-redraw prediction consistency reached 96%.

Those are the two measured results for the held-out ADMG compositions. The 87% figure concerns paired identifiability judgments around confounder edits. The 96% figure concerns whether predictions remain consistent when an ADMG is redrawn equivalently. They measure different behaviors, even though both are reported across the 2,000 held-out compositions.
What does the 87% figure tell me about the edit comparison?

It reports confounder-edit paired accuracy: how often the before-and-after identifiability judgments were correct as a pair under that measurement. The edit is a change to represented confounding, so this result concerns predictions around a structural change. It does not mean that 87% of edits changed the correct identifiability answer.
Why not interpret it as the percentage of edits that flipped the answer?

Because paired accuracy is about the correctness of the judgments, not the frequency of label changes. A confounder edit can alter the graph while the particular causal effect retains the same identifiability status. The reported 87% does not specify how many pairs had matching versus different correct answers.
Then what does the 96% measure?

It reports prediction consistency across equivalent redrawings. Equivalent redrawings depict the same represented ADMG despite looking different, so the comparison asks whether the predictions agree across those presentations. The 96% figure is about agreement, not necessarily about whether each agreed-upon prediction was correct.
Could I describe the redraw result as 96% identifiability accuracy?

No. The stated result is 96% equivalent-redraw prediction consistency. Calling it identifiability accuracy would replace an agreement measure with a correctness measure, which is not what that figure reports.
And calling the 87% figure redraw consistency would mix them up in the other direction?

Yes. The 87% belongs to confounder-edit paired accuracy; the 96% belongs to equivalent-redraw prediction consistency. Keeping the names attached to their respective figures preserves the structural-edit versus unchanged-structure distinction.
